messages.subject: effective sample size vs overdispersion
messages.body_plain:
Dear HM-group,

I just started to learn jags and I´d like to fit an N-mixture model to count data using this framework. I only have few spatial replications but replicated sessions across several years (with 2-5 replications within each session). Therefore I am using time-for-space substitution (if that matters?).

The basic model looks like this:
for (i in 1:nSessions) {
    loglam[i] <- beta0 + beta1*Xi1[i] + ...
    loglam.lim[i] <- min(250, max(-250, loglam[i]))    ############ 'Stabilize' log
    mu.poisson[i] <- exp(loglam.lim[i])
    N[i] ~ dpois(mu.poisson[i])

    for (j in nRepWithinSessions) {
            Cmyo[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N[i])
            p[i,j] <- 1 / (1 + exp(-lp.lim[i,j]))
            lp.lim[i,j] <- min(250, max(-250, lp[i,j]))      ############ 'Stabilize' logit
            lp[i,j] <- alpha0 + alpha1*Xj1[i,j]+ ...
    }
}

My problem/question is the following:

I do face serious overdispersion when using a Poisson variance structure.
In order to reduce overdispersion I tried Negative-binomial, Poisson with Observation-level random effects and Poisson-lognormal instead of a Poisson model. Although overdispersion is greatly reduced (not present at all) in all these cases I ran into problems regarding the effective sample size of the intercepts (alpha0, beta0). I think this is due to autocorrelation (within the chains) and crosscorrelation issues (both present in that cases) but I have no idea how to proceed. Of course I tried different number of iterations and thinning (up to 500.000 iterations with a thinning rate of 150, 3 chains) but things did not change much.

I compared negbin and poisson for an example of simulated data from the AHM1-book and both performed quite well.
I also used unmarked::pcount() for my own data/model and got reasonable results from negbin (again serious overdispersion when using the Poisson variant).

I tried several "levels" of more or less uninformative priors (e.g. dnorm(0, 1e-6) OR dnorm(0, 1e-2) for alpha1, beta1, ...) but again things did not change much (which in principle is a good thing). Unfortunately my experience/knowledge in choosing "good" priors is still quite limited.

I hope someone can point me in the right direction.
Thanks in advance.

Best regards,
Frederik

messages.subject: Bayesian dynamic occupancy residuals ?
messages.body_plain:
Greetings everyone,

I'm interested in computing the residuals for a Bayesian dynamic occupancy model. What are some suggestions on how to go about this? Or has anyone else already figured this out?

Thank you!

Best,
Eve Bohnett
messages.body_snippet:
Greetings everyone,

I'm interested in computing the residuals for a Bayesian dynamic occupancy model. What are some suggestions on how to go about this? Or has anyone else already figured this out?

messages.subject: Re: Bayesian dynamic occupancy residuals ?
messages.body_plain:
Hmm.. just my two cents: I suppose residuals aren't often calculated from generalized linear models, because these models don't have any distributional assumptions about them (i.e., only normal linear models assume your residuals to be normally distributed). You can of course still calculate them anyway.. you would have to work only on the 'detection' level, as that is the only level where you have observed data (0/1). You would use your fitted model to predict (probability of) detections back to where you have observed data, and calculate the difference between expected and observed.
Cheers,
Erica

mean squared error or absolute error (of the residuals) also isn't optimized in binomial models (as it is in ML linear models..) so I'm not even sure you could use that to compare models (or judge model fit?). AUC is a common diagnostic metric for models of binary data though (which is also based on predicted versus observed values).

messages.subject: A Question About Mortality Analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hello Dear All,

I hope you are doing well,

I have systematically collected brown bear mortality cases in Iran (n=147 cases) and I want to use GLMM to analyze it. Kills as a response variable (kill1, kill2, ...) and other information as explanatory variables (sex, age, season, ...) and effort (number of websites reported the news) as an offset. Do you have any comments or ideas on it?

Besides, please let me know if any other methodology or analysis can be conducted with this type of data, I'm keen to learn various analyses concerning population demographics and mortality factors. especially related to these types of datasets.

The questions I want to answer are the relationship between different variables affecting the death of bears and which one is more significant (I want to add some covariates such as forest cover % and ...).

Looking forward to hearing from you,
Cheers,
Danial,

Dear Eve, Marc et al,

R package DHARMa by Florian Hartig implements the randomized quantile residuals of Dunn and Smyth. The focus is frequentist, but there is a function, createDHARMa(), that allows the user to convert externally generated posterior predictive checks into a DHARMa object. I’ve not used the function, but it might be helpful in this context.

Cheers,

Rob

messages.subject: Re: A Question About Mortality Analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Danial,

What values do your response variables take? If it is truly kill1, kill2, ..., that sounds like a categorical response (with only one set of covariate values per response) that will not lend itself to GLMM. If the response is "yes a bear was killed" in every case (1, 1, 1, .....), then there is no variation in the response for the covariates to explain.

Do you have any data for non-mortalities? Or any background data to define what you would expect if bears were killed randomly? If not, it's going to be difficult to determine what covariates are associated with bear mortality, because you won't have anything for comparison.

Maybe someone else has a better idea!

Cheers,

Emily

Emily Weiser (she/her)

https://sites.google.com/site/emilylweiser/
http://birding-by-bike.blogspot.com

> Do you have any data for non-mortalities? Or any background data to define what you would expect if bears were killed randomly? If not, it's going to be difficult to determine what covariates are associated with bear mortality, because you won't have anything for comparison.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Danial,

OK, that looks more like a regression problem now. But your data scheme should look more like this, right ?

site     mortality    other explanatory variables ...
1        3            ....

2        1            ....
3        5            .....

That is, your response is the number of dead bears per 'site' (whatever that is) and you want to explain that with your covariates. If that is the case, then really this looks to me like a simple Poisson GLM. One thing: you mention the number of websites that covered the news as an offset, but another important factor that could be treated as an offset is perhaps the area of what you treat as a site (assuming that your sites are really some sort of region, such as a municipality or park). All things equal, larger areas should produce more dead bears and this would be accommodated as a covariate with value log(area) and a coefficient forced to be 1 (i.e., as an offset).

Best regards  --- Marc
